utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing will resume. Please be seated. Concerning the motion of the Defence presented this morning during the Status Conference which was held -- I'm sorry (Off-the-record discussion with registrar)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, I am rendering a public decision. Concerning the motion of the Defence relating to the prohibition of any prior contact before the witnesses called by the Court come to testify, the Trial Chamber will render the following decision: First, any contact with the Court witnesses, as of today and until their appearance, is prohibited, formally prohibited. We are talking about the Court witnesses, the witnesses concerned in the order of this Trial Chamber filed on the 25th of March. I remind you that we are talking about General Petkovic, General Morillon, General Bob Stewart, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, all commanders of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault. Secondly, these witnesses will be summoned or called by the Trial Chamber right after the end of the Defence case; that is to say, these witnesses will appear here before the Prosecution exercises its rebuttal right and before the rejoinder of the Defence. Thirdly, after the appearance of the Court witnesses, the parties will have the right, within the framework of their rebuttal and rejoinder cases respectively, to call all the witnesses they wish to call, including Court witnesses, if one or both parties judge it necessary. Within the framework of this rejoinder or rebuttal, contact with the witnesses will be authorised. Of course, the Court will still have the right to assess this right according to what the witnesses will have said in front of the Judges. Last point. During the hearing of the Court witnesses, during their testimonies, the parties will be allowed to ask the questions they feel are necessary, and these questions will have to be related to the questions of the Judges in accordance with the order of the 25th of March, but they will have limited time to do so. This time will be set when the witness appears. As a remark, I would like to remind you that after the end of the examination-in-chief of General Blaskic and after the Prosecution's cross-examination and after we hear the last witnesses of the Defence -- and I am turning to Mr. Registrar -- the Court witnesses will have to appear at that particular time, and please inform Mr. Olivier Fourmy of all the procedures engaged in front of all the authorities of the different countries of the various Court witnesses. This being done, we can now turn to the witness. The accused is now testifying and is answering the questions asked by his counsel, Mr. Nobilo. Mr. Nobilo, you can have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Can I have one moment, please? I think it has to do with the French transcript only. If I understood you well, you said in your last comment that both parties would be allowed to ask the witnesses questions, and this was going to relate to what the accused has said but you were thinking about what the witnesses had said. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Yes, of course. Depending upon what the witness would have said, that is, General Blaskic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: No, I think the parties will be allowed to ask questions to the Court witnesses depending upon what the Court witness will have said before and not depending upon what the accused will have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the Court witness, but I was thinking that as far as the accused is concerned, questions will have to be asked on what the accused will have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this remark, Mr. Fourmy. If there are no further comments, then, Mr. Nobilo, I shall turn to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think that before the break of seven days, we were looking into the chronology of events, and we stopped with the 24th of October, 1993

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, if you recall where we left off, please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 24th of October, Your Honours, I had a meeting with the commander of the military police, and I asked him for an investigation with regard to the conflict between two local commanders in Novi Travnik, Tuka and Zuti, and I also sought an investigation for the security assistant with relation to the same event. At the time, I was informed that disciplinary measures were taken against two policemen, that they were in a prison, in detention, and I was called from 12.00 to 1.00 to attend a meeting with the head of the centre for the security service for the Vitez area, Mr. Miso Mijic, who informed me at the meeting about the cadres question, personnel in the centre for security, the head office for security, and supervision over helicopter flights and other issues that were discussed, and emphasis was laid on the fact that the security service centre was directly under the office in Mostar and that it was independent with regard to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we stop there for a minute and have these documents handed round, and may we have a number for the documents, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D552 for the Croatian version and D552A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The text is short, and I will read out the main points. The document is from the defence department, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone SIS, Security and Information Service, the date is the 18th of June, 1993. It is a military secret and was sent to Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, that is, yourself, the zone commander, and the title is "Authorisation." (as read) "Further to the order number 02-4/1-533/93 of the 19th of March, 1993, of Assistant Chief Mr. Ivica Lucic on the formation of the Central Bosnia SIS Centre, which gives Mr. Miso Mijic, the head of the centre, a free hand in selecting his associates and about which you have been informed and with the purpose of improving the work of the Central Bosnia SIS Centre, I hereby appoint Colonel Darko Kraljevic as the Deputy Chief of the Central Bosnia SIS Centre and at the same time authorise him to sign letters, reports, orders and other documents pertaining to the work of the Central Bosnia SIS Centre whenever the need arises." The signature is the Central Bosnia SIS Centre, Chief Miso Mijic, signed and stamped the Mostar Defence Department, and so on. There is a sentence at the end which states that: "The Mostar Defence Department has been advised of the above decision so we are hereby forwarding it to you for your information." That is the last sentence of the document. On the basis of this document, I would to ask you first: Do you recognise the stamp and the signature of Miso Mijic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the stamp. It is the Security and Information Service, the defence department of Mostar, that is the stamp. I know Miso Mijic and I know his signature and that is his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th of June, 1993, or around that date, did you receive a letter of this kind from Miso Mijic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I received this particular document probably around that date, the 18th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber, on the basis of this document and on the basis of your recollections, were you able in any way to influence the organisation of the Security and Information Service and their selection of personnel, and tell us, please, in what way did Darko Kraljevic come to have the same rank as you yourself and what authorisation did Darko Kraljevic and Miso Mijic have in setting up this SIS centre?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have any authorisation or competence over the SIS Centre. The SIS Centre was directly subordinate with regard to chain of command to the head office of the security service, and it was not duty-bound even to inform me of their activities, intentions, and tasks and assignments. Colonel Darko Kraljevic, as the commander of the special purpose unit, the Vitezovi, which was also directly subordinate to the defence department in Mostar, had the rank of colonel. This information, this document shows that along with his task of commander of the special purpose unit, he was assigned another task, and that is, he was deputy of the chief of the SIS Centre for Central Bosnia, with authorisations that are precisely defined in this authorisation, this particular document. Therefore, they worked completely independently of me and the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already told the Court that in individual battles, the Vitezovi of Darko Kraljevic was attached to you. Could you please tell the Court, this new function of Darko Kraljevic, what did it mean for his independence vis-à-vis you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it meant that his independence was enormously enlarged, and his powers of command, because with the new function that he took over for the entire region of Central Bosnia, he became the Number 2 man of the Security and Information Service, that is to say, the secret service, which did not have any responsibilities towards the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command, and it was, in its functioning, completely independent and autonomous with regard to that command, so this new function increased the already high powers of command of the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This independent SIS Centre, did it have any power of control over you, over your command and your staff in the command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course it did because it was a secret service and it held informative interviews with my associates, it would take them in for questioning and for interviewing, and I remember that some of my associates complained to me and said that they were not able to carry out the tasks that I had assigned to them because they had received invitations to obligatorily attend the informative talks with the officials at the SIS Centre, and also the officers from the command of the HVO brigades, the service would take them in too without informing me of this fact, and it would control, in terms of security, the entire command, so it would select the methods it used itself and select the cadres and personnel that it wanted to interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To round off the topic, with the formation of this new service of the SIS centre with Darko Kraljevic there, was your power of command in the Lasva River Valley increased or decreased?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was considerably decreased, and the overall situation also became more complex, much more complicated. I found the situation very difficult because my powers of command were greatly reduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue with the chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the course of the day, I worked with the commander of the military police. On the 24th of October we worked on the elaboration of a plan of action against criminal groups in the Lasva pocket. On the 25th of October, 1993, at the morning briefing, the assistant for security informed me that high officials from the head office for security had come to visit the Lasva pocket and that they were checking the results of the investigation into the crime committed in Ahmici. I also had a meeting in the course of the day, that is to say, in the course of the 25th of October, with the command of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade. On the 26th of October, 1993, when the UNHCR convoy was moving under the escort of the BritBat battalion and its forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General Blaskic. Did you meet these high officials who came to see if all the orders given in the course of the investigation had been executed? Did you meet these officials?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They never contacted me. The officials from the head office for security never contacted me, those which came to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. They never contacted me, and they didn't contact me on that occasion either. They just controlled their own services. I did not have a meeting with them, nor did they contact me at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, General, the events of the 25th of October.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 26th of October, 1993, as I have said, a convoy of the UNHCR was moving from the direction of Gornji Vakuf towards Novi Travnik, Vitez, and Zenica. The convoy was escorted by UNPROFOR. A sabotage group of the 7th Muslim Brigade took advantage of this movement of the convoy and infiltrated itself into the head of the convoy and stormed the village of Rastovci in the Novi Travnik municipality. In that village of Rastovci these people killed seven civilians, opening fire on the village and locals of the village. It was only after the military police intervened that this sabotage group of the 7th Muslim Brigade was made to retreat towards Ravno Rostovo. I also received information in the course of the day that in Vitez itself Commander Tuka had been killed. He was from the composition of the Travnik Brigade and that the suspects, the perpetrators -- the suspects were Ferdo Gazibaric, and two Biljaka brothers, and Ilija Dobodza, and they had all fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let's stop there, pause there. Would you please remind us why Commander Tuka was killed? The killers and the victims, were they of the same ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, both the killers and the victim were Croats. Commander Tuka had previously, in Novi Travnik, and I have already spoken about this, wounded one of the chiefs of a local group there, Mr. Zuti, and then there was the settling of accounts and revenge was taken on him probably by the followers of Zuti. They wanted to revenge themselves on Commander Tuka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the course of the day, I was informed by the assistant for information and propaganda that Radio Zenica, which was under the control of the BH army, was constantly broadcasting news over the radio on the crime committed in Stupni Do, and I had a talk with the main staff and asked for information about that event and what had happened in Stupni Do. I had received information that there had been a conflict. A conflict had broken out between the HVO and the BH army, and that it was a purely combat operation with the participation of members of the HVO and the BH army. In the course of the day I had a talk with the followers of Colonel Tuka, who were from the Travnik Brigade, and I tried to reduce tensions and to take preventative measures in order to prevent a mutual settling of accounts between the members of the Frankopan and Travnik Brigades, for the most part. At 15.00, I had a meeting with an official from the Red Cross, but I have not noted his name so I cannot remember his name at the moment. The questions that we discussed on the occasion were the following: The freeing of the detained Croats, the free passage towards Stari Vitez, and I clarified, for the purposes of the Red Cross officials, the fact that it was necessary for us to receive, at least one day in advance, notification of the passage of the International Red Cross in the area of Stari Vitez which was under the control of the BH army because, otherwise, without this advance notice it would be impossible for us to demine the front line, because our positions were subject to direct sniper fire from the BH army. Therefore, I asked them if this was at all possible, to inform us of their intention to enter Stari Vitez and give us that information one day in advance, and that no other limitations with regard to entry existed, at least from the part of the HVO. The problem was that you had to pass -- either when entering or exiting -- you had to pass at least two front lines. One line was the HVO front line and the other front line was the BH army front line. I also asked the officials of the International Red Cross to try to tour the area of Vares and to send me information if it had any information about the situation in Vares and especially the events that had taken place in Stupni Do. I was promised by the officials of the International Red Cross that they would indeed visit the area and send me the information that they were able to collect regarding this matter. So we discussed the timing for a lecture for HVO commanders on the topic of the International Red Cross, its mandate, the Geneva Conventions, and international war law. This was a promise made to me by representatives of international organisations that they would organise this seminar, and I requested that the date be fixed for that seminar. An officer of the International Red Cross told me that it would take place within a period of seven days, at the latest. I also informed the International Red Cross of the killing of seven civilians in the village of Rastovci, Novi Travnik municipality, by a sabotage group of the 7th Muslim Brigade. On the 27th of October, 1993, at about 10.00, I had a meeting with Colonel Duncan. We discussed quite a wide range of issues, one of them being the incursion of a sabotage terrorist group of the 7th Muslim Brigade on the previous day into the village of Rastovci. I underlined, speaking to Colonel Duncan, the security problems we were encountering because at checkpoints the HVO military police did not stop nor check UNPROFOR vehicles as well as vehicles of the UNHCR, and other vehicles that were white in colour and which belonged to international organisations. However, we had already been informed that some of those vehicles had been hijacked and that they were being used for incursions and sabotage operations such as the ones carried out in Rastovci and Novi Travnik. I expressed my concern that such incidents could be become more numerous, especially during the night. At that meeting with Colonel Duncan, I asked him to check on the report that I had received about the execution of 30 Croats in Jeljezno Polje on the road between Zenica and Zepce, by the BH army. These were mobilised conscripts, Croats, which the BH army had mobilised, and they had refused to take part in combat operations against the HVO of Zepce. I did not receive any confirmation of this report from Colonel Duncan. At that meeting, I also asked for greater supplies of fuel which we were receiving for the needs of the hospital, as the Lasva pocket was without electricity. So we used that fuel to operate the generator in the church-cum-hospital during operations. We also discussed the passage of the Tuzla convoy, that is, the convoy carrying military equipment for the BH army which passed unhindered through the area of the Lasva pocket. In the course of that day, I reviewed the security in the explosives factory, that is where the security was provided by members of the military police, and I again attended a meeting of the brigade command in Busovaca where we had a series of problems related to the abandoning of front lines on the part of HVO soldiers. These incidents were carried out in groups, collectively, and this was a threat to the security of our positions and the security of the overall defence of the area of Busovaca under HVO control. There were various proposals made by members of the command, including the proposal that radical measures should be taken, that is, that such individuals should be executed to set an example. I reacted resolutely and said that executions were out of the question but that we should continue to read my orders, to frighten the soldiers, and to tell them that this was one of the possibilities that could be resorted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're talking about front lines, Mr. Blaskic. You're saying that the soldiers left the front lines. I would like more details. Are you talking about the front lines against the Serbs or against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, I am talking about the front line towards the BH army. The front lines indicated here on the relief but for the area of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 28th of October, 1993, I received a report from the military police that a car that had been seized by force had been returned by the military police from the Vitezovi and that this vehicle had been returned to its owner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that exception when you took note of this, of the return of this vehicle from the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of the miracles and this was a test for the military police. It was certainly an exception and a rarity. At 10.30, I had a meeting with brigade commanders in the Lasva pocket. We reviewed the overall question of defence, the questions regarding desertion on the front lines, the fatigue of personnel. I also addressed a message to all followers of one of the criminal groups, that they should report to the defence department in order to be given a war time assignment. This was, in fact, the beginning of the implementation of our plan to disarm and eliminate criminal groups operating in the Lasva pocket. This was a form of selective pressure against one of such group. On the 29th of October, 1993, I was engaged in training in the military police practically the whole day, starting from reviewing military police ranks, then the question of organisation of the military police, the technique of control and command. At a meeting with the military police, I requested that they inform me what had happened with the investigation into the murder of the interpreter Dobrila. Actually, I demanded to know the names of the suspects, but I did not receive a report at that meeting of the names of the suspects for that murder. On the 31st of October, 1993, early in the morning, we had a severe attack launched by the BH army on the town of Vitez coming from the directions of Kruscica, Sljibcica, Stari Vitez, and Zabrdze towards the explosives factory. In the course of the day, I also received a request from the assistant for logistics who informed me that they were short of food for children or, rather, that we had one kilogram of powdered milk for a large number of children available for that day. On the 1st of November, 1993, we were encountering difficulties in control and command which was being blocked, especially in neighbouring brigades. For instance, in the Frankopan Brigade, we were unable to regroup and to transfer a minimum number of ten soldiers to assist the people on the front lines for we were already in such a situation that the soldiers had trenches in their own back yards and nobody wanted to abandon his own home and join in the defence of the front lines where military logic required it, such as the front line at Vitez. Also on the 1st of November, in the Vitez Hotel, officials of the International Red Cross held a lecture, which had been agreed previously, and during that lecture on the mandate of the International Red Cross, the Geneva Conventions, and international law of war, there were about 30 officers from the Lasva Valley attending. On the 2nd of November, I received information that the supporters of Tuka's unit from the Travnik Brigade had abandoned their positions on the front line facing the BH army and that they were preparing to take their revenge on the followers of Zuti. I held another meeting with some of those members trying to persuade them that revenge would not be a solution and that the only way out was to carry out an investigation into that killing. In the course of the day, I also had a meeting with the commander of the military police, trying to find a solution to this problem and the threats of revenge and also trying to find a solution to deal with the criminal groups and the potential of their mutual showdowns. The greatest problem was how to disarm those gangs. I received information from the assistant for logistics that the only foodstuffs available were rice and lentils and that the situation was extremely critical in terms of food supply as well as in terms of materiel and equipment for combat operations. I was also informed that talks were ongoing with representatives of the 3rd Corps through mediators from international organisations and that there were indications that the 3rd Corps, with a commission of 30 per cent of the war tax, would allow the passage of a food convoy to reach the Lasva pocket. However, that convoy never arrived. There was also a serious shortage of cigarettes and fuel, and at the time, a box of cigarettes in the Lasva Valley cost between 60 and 100 German marks, and a litre of fuel, about six, going up to ten, German marks. On that day, at Sljibcica, elevation 592, the BH army destroyed an electric pillar whereby it further complicated the situation regarding power supply for the Lasva Valley. As for combat operations, they were most intensive in Novi Travnik in the immediate vicinity of the Stojkovici logistics base where the positions of the HVO and the BH army went along the very fence of that logistics base. At 21.15, I spoke to the chief of the main staff by phone and I informed him that the situation in the Lasva Valley was extremely critical and that we were about to fall and I asked him whether he had any information regarding developments in Vares and what was happening there and also as to what was happening in Stupni Do. The reply I received was that I should not worry but that I should continue working and trying to defend the Lasva pocket. I also inquired into the situation in Kiseljak and asked whether it was possible for operations to be engaged in from Kiseljak towards the BH army so as to alleviate the pressure on the front lines in the Lasva pocket or, if possible, to deblock the Busovaca-Kiseljak road. I said that in the Lasva enclave, there was hunger, and that the combat operations were highly intensive and that I didn't know how we would endure. The chief of staff told me that he would look into it and he would do what he could from Kiseljak and that he would try and assist us. On the 3rd of November, 1993, I was informed that at 11.00, Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian organisation under that name, was entering Stari Vitez with ambulances, and the HVO assisted in their arrival and entry into Stari Vitez. Again, we reorganised the defence sectors for the town of Vitez in particular and the remaining area under HVO control because the pressure was particularly strong on the town of Vitez, that is, the explosives factory. I also received a request on the 3rd of November from the church-cum-hospital in Nova Bila, from the manager of that hospital, Dr. Tihomir Peric, that there were 86 severely wounded patients in the hospital and that all of them needed to be evacuated from the hospital. On the 4th of November, 1993, at the morning meeting with the commander of the military police, I insisted again that all military conscripts, for which such an order was issued by the district military court in Vitez, have to be processed regardless of their positions on the front lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The French booth -- I think that the French booth is a little bit late. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We will have to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think the French booth is using the transcript, isn't it? By the way, we will take a break because we have to stop a little bit early today. But, please, slow down, General, for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Forgive me. I asked for all the military conscripts to be processed regardless of their place and role at the front line. My position was that without them, we would manage to defend ourselves just as well. At 11.45, I received information from the IPD assistant that Radio Zenica, which was under control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was saying that the town of Vares was liberated by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. During the day, with my co-workers, I talked about command responsibility and the problems that we had and familiarity and also that there were certain groups that were privileged in respect of the commanders. On the 5th of November, 1993, an anti-sabotage unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina made an incursion from the area of Zabrdze into the explosives factory in Vitez. So for quite a long time that day, we were fighting just by the fence of that explosives factory, on the southern side, near the warehouse for explosives. There were hundreds of tonnes of explosives there, and we were worried, we were afraid that one of these warehouses might be activated. From 18.00 until 24.00, the same problem was repeated with the Frankopan Brigade, which did not manage to send help to Vitez, and the entire brigade was supposed to send only ten soldiers to help fortify the positions at the Vitez front line. During the course of the day, a lady called me, she did not introduce herself by her name, but she said that she was the wife of Abdulah Tuco, and she phoned me and asked for protection and help, saying that in her family home in Rijeka, House No. 5, there were unknown men who were barging into her house and who were expelling her and her family from the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, General, what was the ethnic background of the Abdulah Tuco family?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were Muslims, Bosniaks. They lived in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you react?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that moment, I immediately dispatched my driver and one of my escorts to give help and protection to this lady, the wife of Abdulah Tuco, and I told her that I was sending my driver right away, because I didn't have anyone else. I also called Commander Mario Cerkez, and I issued an order to him to send a patrol, a guard, there, and to place them in the immediate vicinity of that house, and that the guards should report to that family, the Tuco family, and to tell them that their task was to protect that family from other persecutions and incursions of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will stop ten minutes early today and we will resume at 2.45. Mr. Harmon, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll be very, very brief. I just would like to raise a matter of clarification with the judgment, the decision that was raised by the Court. First off, I want to let you know that we accept the judgment of the Court and we're not contesting it and we're not trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (No interpretation)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think the judgment would preclude -- under the terms of the judgment would preclude the Kordic team, for example, from having any contact with witnesses whom they may well intend to call in their case in chief and they may well intend to call those witnesses before the Court has an opportunity to listen to those witnesses, and I understand the thrust of the Chamber, in its decision, it would be that the Blaskic Prosecutors not contact these witnesses, but I would like some clarification as to whether or not the Chamber's order applies equally to the Prosecutors who are involved and will commence next week the Kordic prosecution because that raises and may well raise certain problems for the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (No interpretation) ... the Chamber cannot rule regarding other cases. ... matter further, if need be, but, of course, this Trial Chamber cannot decide in other cases. Of course, the Prosecution, I'm sure, is trying to have contact with certain witnesses in other cases, and I am sorry to learn that there was this coincidence that maybe the three witnesses, or at least Colonel Stewart, are witnesses that the Office of the Prosecutor is trying to contact at the moment. I will just add that the Trial Chamber does not want any contact with Colonel Stewart, Mr. Thebault, General Morillon, Mr. Hadzihasanovic, et cetera, within the framework of the summons of these witnesses that will appear in the following days or weeks, we don't want any contact, in the framework of the Blaskic case, of course. I can't forbid you to go and see these witnesses, but I just warn you, Mr. Prosecutor, if, during these contacts, you take this opportunity to try to exert pressure or to contact these witnesses on the content of their testimony in the Blaskic case, then it will be your responsibility and this will be against the order that we rendered. But the rest -- I mean, I can't and I don't think my colleagues can forbid any kind of contact with witnesses in the framework of other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As I said when I started my inquiry, Mr. President, I fully accept the decision of the Chamber. The Prosecutor's Office does not want to find itself in a position where prosecutors from the Kordic team, in the presentation of their case in chief, have got to contact these witnesses, and later I hear a complaint that the Prosecutor's Office has violated this Court's order. What I am seeking is absolute clarity in order to avoid a potential problem. As I understand, is I understand the Chamber to say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's very simple, Mr. Harmon, if you want to be reassured. First of all, this is a question of ethics which is submitted to the constant control of the Chamber. Secondly, I will ask the registry and Mr. Fourmy that the meaning of this decision be transmitted to all the witnesses who have been summoned, and Colonel Stewart will know what he should expect if the Office of the Prosecutor needed to contact him before. Therefore, he will know what kind of questions he is allowed to answer and what kind of questions he should not answer, and I will make sure that this is done when Colonel Stewart comes to testify here. I will ask him, "Did you have any contact with the Office of the Prosecutor within the framework of the Blaskic case?" And since he will be taking the oath, he will have to tell the truth. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So as I understand it, to make it perfectly clear, if the Kordic team contacts these witnesses in respect of the Kordic case, that will be permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is none of my business. I just want to warn you that there may be some interference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break, we spoke about the 5th of November, 1993. General, would you please continue and tell us about the last two months, in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, on the 5th of November I received information that the special purpose unit, Tvrtko, had left the front line facing the BH army and of its own free will returned to base. About this event on the event of the 5th of November, I informed, in writing, the chief of the main staff and asked once again for them to allow me a reorganisation of the special purpose units and a change in structure for those units, and that the special purpose units be directly subordinate in the chain of command to the command of the Operative Zone during the encirclement, at that particular time. On the 6th of November, 1993, the BH army launched a strong offensive from its southern positions in relation to the town of Vitez and the explosives factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What were the results? You requested the reorganisation of special purpose units. What was the response you got?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, on that day and in that month I did not receive an answer from the chief of the main staff, but later on I did receive authorisation, and I will come to that as I go through the chronology of events, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 6th of November, 1993, there was a strong attack from the southern positions where the BH army continued to repel the HVO towards the explosives factory. In that attack we sustained losses, that is to say, we lost 71 soldiers, that is to say, 6 were skilled, 17 wounded, and 48 were missing. Later on, it was established that 43 of the 48 men were living. It was determined that they were alive. In the afternoon, after we had succeeded in consolidating our ranks at new positions, I once again had, in the military police, a meeting and training with parts of the units of the military police, that is to say, we trained them for military police assignments, for patrol work, and I tried to gain an insight into how the units were manned with the new recruits, which we took for the most part from the front lines and from the defence lines to fill up the ranks. In the course of the evening, I issued a task to the logistics assistant to undertake the dislocation of explosives from the warehouse of the explosives factory and to take them to provisional warehouses and bases towards Novi Travnik and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, what was the reason you wanted to evacuate from the explosives factory at the time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the reason for that was the danger that due to combat operations and fighting, which already took place at the approaches to the warehouses in the explosives factory, that there could have been a detonation, an activation of one of the warehouses. As there were hundreds of tonnes of explosives there, about 500.000 tonnes of explosives approximately, and all the warehouses of the explosives were, for the most part -- that is to say, 50 to 100 metres away from the front, which meant that a sabotage unit could activate one of those warehouses, set them on fire. This could also have happened through fighting, that there could have been self-activation in the explosives warehouses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that particular day, that is to say, the 6th of November, I spent most of the day in Gornja and Donja Veceriska, upper and lower Veceriska, that part of the front. On the 7th of November, I went to the front line, which was Sector 1, and it was the village of Zaselje in actual fact. When I toured that front line I ascertained that of the 90 soldiers that I saw up at the front line, 30 soldiers did not have any kind of weapons whatsoever and they, for the most part, were used to take out the injured and wounded. If any of the soldiers were to have been killed, then they would have taken over the weapons and rifles of those killed soldiers and taken up their positions. So we still needed many more weapons to man that part of the front line. On the 8th of November, 1993, we organised new positions and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you slow down a bit, please, General,? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So south of the explosives factory we had positions there and would move some 50 to 100 metres. We moved slowly and withdrew gradually towards the explosive factory itself and the fence there because of the attacks from the BH army. On the 9th of November, 1993, I received information that the new chief of the main staff of the HVO was appointed and he was General Colonel Ante Roso. On the 10th of November, 1993, in Gornja Veceriska, I had a meeting with the commanders of the sectors, and the topic we discussed was the defence of the access to the explosives factory, but once again, at that meeting, the commanders of the special purpose units did not attend the meeting. We were not able to find them to tell them to come to the meeting. Also on that day I received information from the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, and he said that during the 9th of November, on that particular day, the BH army had launched three attacks towards the Kaonik crossroads, that is to say, on the main road, the Vitez-Busovaca-Zenica main road. This information came to us one day late, almost a whole day late. Once again, with my associates, I looked into the need to reorganise the defence of the Lasva pocket and to reorganise the forces, the defence forces, for the area. I worked on elaborating a proposal for a new chief of the main staff, that is to say, in the sense of reorganising the special purpose units and reorganisation for the guard units which would be under my direct command. This proposal I sent on the 10th of November, 1993 to the chief of the main staff of the HVO, but I did not receive a response, an answer, to my proposal immediately. We also saw that individual group of the special purpose units were seeking money. They wanted to be remunerated and paid to be involved up at the front line. They asked for money from the wealthy individuals, and they asked them to pay for their services. The BH army, in the course of the day, used snipers and mortars, 60-millimetre mortars, from Old Vitez and artillery fire from Sljibcica, and Sivrino Selo, and Kruscica. That is where the firing came from. On the 11th of November, 1993, we assessed our possibilities to man the guard units in the Lasva pocket. The foundations for that would be the special purpose units, they would be the foundation for this, and recruits up to the age of 35, conscripts up to the age of 35. I also attended a meeting that was held at the Vitez Hotel, and the topic of that meeting was public law and order and how to suppress crime generally. It was a coordination meeting in character, and I was there as the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, I should like to follow what you are saying because this is important for me. You engaged more men from the special purpose units. You required more men from the special purpose units, but what is important is what happened afterwards. What was the reaction? "I requested men from the special purpose unit to go to the front." My question is: What was the result of that request? Are you going to come to that later?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall be speaking about this later, but I just wanted to mention that on the 9th of November a new chief of the main staff of the HVO arrived, and for that reason I once again had to elaborate a proposal for the reorganisation of the special purpose units. In my chronology of events, I will say when that reorganisation took place, that is to say, when I received permission from the chief of the main staff to undertake the reorganisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not authorisation, it is the terminology you're using. So please be careful. We're following very closely. "I took a decision to deploy more men coming from the special units." It was a decision that you take. It was not a proposal, it was a decision. Maybe it was due to an erroneous translation. Mr. Nobilo, perhaps you can help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I can help you. I think the translation was not precise enough. The General said that with his associates, he elaborated a plan for the creation of a new unit which would include individuals from the special purpose units and men up to the age of 35. So that was a plan on paper still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You told me very well, Mr. Nobilo, but you are not the witness. General Blaskic, is that what you wanted to say, "which one include" in the conditional tense; is that right? So please be very precise because I want to know what is specific. If it is a plan that you elaborated, we will see the results later on. If you actually engage men, that's something else. So what Mr. Nobilo has told us is that you drafted a plan for the new chief of staff, a plan which would include, in the conditional, the engagement of men coming from the special purpose unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can repeat what I said. I am referring to the 10th of November, 1993 -- things are much clearer to me now -- and I reviewed with my associates the need to determine reorganisation, to look at a new organisation for the units, which would include the abolition of the special purpose units and have a new formation of a guard unit which would be under the direct command of the Operative Zone. A plan of this kind, that kind of plan, I sent to the new chief of the main staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good thing, General, in order to clarify matters and make things clearer to all of us, and particularly the Trial Chamber, if you could recall the dates when the individual chiefs of staff were performing their duty because during 1993 this post was taken over by several individuals? So could you tell us the dates when they were the chief and when they ceased to be?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: According to my recollection -- I don't know the exact date when General Petkovic was replaced by General Praljak, who was the new chief of the main staff, but at the end of September 1993, I had a meeting with General Praljak and he was performing the role of the chief of the main staff. General Praljak, according to my own notes, was replaced by General Roso on the 9th of November, 1993. So that was the third chief of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you repeat your concept for the creation of an army and abolishing the special purpose units to each of the chiefs of the main staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I had to do so in order to inform them of the situation and to effect a change in the structure itself because it was my intention to change the structure which was created and established probably by the defence ministry or the main staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on with our chronology of events and draw closer to the time when you succeeded in abolishing the special purpose units.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We stopped with the 11th of November, 1993, when I had a meeting devoted to public law and order and the suppression of crime generally, and that meeting was attended by the commander of the military police and the chief of the police head office of Travnik, the civilian police, also the deputy for security attended the meeting, and it was a meeting at which we elaborated a plan for disarming eight leading criminals in the Lasva pocket together with their supporters. At the meeting, we also highlighted the problem of falsifying medical certificates which were issued to young men saying they were not able to perform their military service and thus these young people wanted to avoid doing military service up at the front lines facing the BH army. On the 12th of November, 1993, there was heavy fighting again, especially along the southern access to the explosives factory in the Vitez Brigade, and the fighting took place at 100 metres away from the explosives factory. In the afternoon, somewhere about 16.30 hours, I received information that my father had died, and I asked the liaison officer, Mr. Gelic, to send a written request to the command of the BritBat to ask the commander to organise transport for me so that I could attend the funeral in Kiseljak, my father's funeral there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, how and when did your father die?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My father was killed in the Kiseljak area, the village is named Oglavak, and it is at the front line between the HVO and the BH army. He was in a trench. He went out of the trench to help a soldier of the HVO who had stepped on a mine and his feet were blown off and he was lying there helpless. I don't know whether my late father tried to pull him out of that position or just to see to his wounds, but my father was hit by a sniper from a 762 rifle from behind and he was shot in the heart. It was just one bullet and he was dead on the spot. He was hit by this machine gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your father when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My father was almost 61 years of age, so that he was not a military recruit, according to the laws of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come he was in the trench? Was he a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was a volunteer because that was the situation at the time, and everything I'm telling you about the Lasva pocket was the same or similar in the area in which he found himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did UNPROFOR enable you to attend your father's funeral?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it did not, and that is why I asked for a meeting with Colonel Duncan, to be able to ask him personally for him to do that. I said that I needed this only on that particular occasion for that particular purpose and that I needed no other assistance apart from being transported from Vitez to the cemetery in Kiseljak and to bring me back. Colonel Duncan said that he did not have agreement from the BH army for a favour of this kind, and were he to do so without the knowledge of the BH army, he would have violated his officer's code.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any way of going to the funeral without UNPROFOR transporting you in one of its vehicles?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, had I had some other way of getting there, I would have, but I had no way of getting there and so I did not go to the funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 13th of November, 1993, I received information that -- rather, I got some information from the Military Intelligence Service that two friars had been killed in Fojnica, in the monastery in Fojnica, and through Gelic, the liaison officer, I asked UNPROFOR to check on this piece of information. The information later proved to be true. Also on that day I sent in the entire security of the command of the Operative Zone to the front line because we were sustaining great losses, and this was indeed necessary, these soldiers were needed at the front line. Before the night or, rather, during the night between the 13th and the 14th, we carried out our first action, armed action, against a group of criminals. When the military police called out to them, they started shooting at them, and during this shoot-out, there were people who were killed and wounded during this action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why is it only on the 13th of November that you decided to take arms against one of these leading gangs of criminals? Why couldn't you do it earlier?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it could not have been done earlier because, first and foremost, the military police as such had to be established in order to be capable of reacting towards criminals in this way, and from August until November, I tried to organise, set up, and train the military police unit for its regular military police work, including, regrettably, things like this as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This kind of armed conflict where the military police of the HVO, that is to say, Croats, attacked other armed Croats in the Lasva Valley, what kind of an effect did all this have on other armed gangs, on the Vitezovi and the other independent units?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, later, this turned out to be very favourable because it was no longer necessary to carry out such large-scale operations because these were indeed the eight leading criminals in the region and this was a showdown with their followers. I actually had a press conference on this occasion too, and we showed some of the weapons and military equipment that we had seized as well as other things. So all of this had a favourable effect on the overall security situation and in terms of paralysing all other gangs in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed with your chronology.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th of November, 1993, as I said, I had a press conference, and we showed some of the weapons and military equipment that were taken from the group of criminals, and we also commented on this action a bit, we explained its point and the need to have it carried out. In the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. When you say "at the press conference," could you please remind us a bit what the main way was of informing the soldiers and citizens in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the main way of doing so was through a press conference which we held at least once a week and then the local television broadcast the contents of this press conference, from one press conference to another, so every family and every soldier in the Lasva River Valley could see the pictures but also hear the most important pieces of information of the events in the past period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please proceed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the afternoon, on the 15th of November, I had a meeting with the representative of the Serbs from Vitez. This gentleman's name was Risto. He asked me whether he and some friends of his could be relieved of duty because they had some health problems so they couldn't carry out their obligations at the front lines, and he also sought assistance, he did specifically, he asked for boots and the others asked for some other parts of military equipment, and I helped him resolve these problems, I accommodated him. Again on the 15th of November, I spent some time with the Travnik Brigade. This unit was made up of refugees for the most part, and I also received information that groups of Vitezovi had barged into the command of the 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade and that they took away an automatic rifle, automatic rifles, rather, and a pistol and cigarettes for soldiers of the 1st Battalion. At that time, we distributed cigarettes in the following manner: an amount of tobacco contained in one cigarette would be allocated to a group of three soldiers, that is to say, there was a great shortage of cigarettes. The same group of Vitezovi attacked the house of Ivo Lozancic in Vitez. He is a Croat too. I asked the military police to give me information about these events and these attacks, and at that time I was informed that the investigation of these events would be carried out by the military police of the Vitezovi unit. Since I knew that there was no such police, I called the commander and I asked him for an explanation. How come there was now a military police of the Vitezovi? I asked who had set up this military police, and the commander of the Vitezovi, Colonel Kraljevic, Colonel Darko Kraljevic, said that he had set up a military police unit which would only take care of the members of the Vitezovi. I asked him what the basis for this was. On the basis of which document did he establish that military police unit? He answered that he did not have to report to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you think about this, General? How come now, in mid-November, 1993, Darko Kraljevic established a military police of the Vitezovi? Now, when you view this from this time distance, what was the reason, the underlying reason?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is certain that one of the reasons was his position but, on the other hand, probably an effort was being made to exclude his members from the jurisdiction of the 4th Battalion or, rather, the 7th Battalion, at that time, which was under my direct command, and they tried and succeeded, to the largest possible extent, to carry out its military police duties. By establishing a Vitezovi military police, the members of the Special Purpose Unit Vitezovi were excluded from the jurisdiction of the 7th Battalion of the HVO and, in a way, they got a privileged status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 16th of November, 1993, once again the family home of Ivo Livancic was attacked, and the IPD, during the 16th of November, organised a tour of the explosives factory with a foreign TV crew. I think the TV was called ITN, but I'm not sure about the name. This TV crew filmed part of the explosives factory that was partly mined, and the intention was to try to send a message to the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that it was pointless to attack the explosives factory. Through this propaganda message, an attempt would be made to alleviate the pressure on the Vitez front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the IPD officer tell the journalists? What was your intention? Why did you mine the explosives factory?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Earlier on, an explanation had been given that if the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were to capture the factory, the factory would be blown up. That is to say that all the explosives in the factory would be activated. However, the largest part of the explosives we had already gotten out of the factory, and we had relocated it to other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At 15.00, I had a meeting with an UNHCR official. They asked me to guarantee safe passage to humanitarian convoys through the Lasva pocket towards Zenica, Zepce, and Maglaj. I informed them that personally I had difficulties in communicating with Zepce but that I would do my best to make it possible for these convoys to pass, that is to say, to the limits to which I can guarantee their safety. Another question that we discussed, and that is what I had brought up when talking to the UNHCR officials, that was the Lasva pocket itself, that is to say, the military setting, and also the fact that there was a lack of power, water, and food. Also, the officials of the UNHCR, and I think that there was a UN official there too, they asked for my permission to have two soldiers evacuated from Stari Vitez to Zenica. I agreed at that meeting and that was done subsequently. On the 17th of November, 1993, I got permission from the chief of the main staff of the HVO to start reorganising the special purpose unit of the B-type. There was only one such unit in the Lasva pocket and that was the PPN Tvrtko. That is to say that this could be reorganised into the home guard brigades of the HVO. Also, on that day I received information that a group from the Vitezovi Special Purpose Unit barged into the house of Branko Mlakic, as far as back as the 15th of November, 1993, but I received this information only on the 17th of November. In the afternoon, I worked on a proposal made by the mayor of Vitez, and his decision to close down shops. Namely, in order to improve the general security situation in the territory of the town of Vitez, the civilian authorities, the municipal government of Vitez, passed a decision to set a limit on the time during which catering establishments could be opened. That related to civilians and also to the military police. However, since the decision passed by the civilian government of Vitez was not obligatory in terms of soldiers, the mayor asked me to issue an order too, by which I would formally confirm this decision of theirs and which would then pertain to all soldiers in the Lasva pocket. I did issue such an order imposing a time limit on the opening hours of cafes and restaurants in Vitez. I also received information that there were still private exchanges in terms of local criminal elements and that they were receiving money for this, but I also received information that such private exchanges were being carried out by members of UNPROFOR too, and also the International Red Cross, and the UNHCR, and even the representatives of the civilian authorities, according to their own criteria. I received this information from the assistant for security matters. At 15.45 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Private exchanges? What do you mean when you use the term "private exchanges?"

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are exchanges that take place apart from the municipal/civilian commission that is in charge of these matters. Individuals come and take away family members. I'll give you a specific example from Vitez. For example, they would take Muslims from Vitez to Zenica, members of their family, and from Zenica they would also being in civilians, family members of Croats, to Vitez, but the municipal civilian commission of Vitez, predominantly Croat, was not informed about this, nor the civilian commission for exchanges in Zenica that was predominantly Muslim. That is to say that these two commissions were not involved in such exchanges. Military commands weren't either, only if the security and intelligence would find out about this through secret channels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, General, as far as these private exchanges are concerned, were these civilians forced to go from Zenica to Vitez or vice versa, or was it actually in the hands of these civilians to take the initiative to go away?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In 99 per cent of all cases -- in most cases, it is the civilians themselves who took this initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they often have to pay for this exchange, for them to be organised?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had received such information that these services were paid for, especially these groups of criminals made quite a profit in such dealings, but this did not happen only in the Lasva pocket. I was aware of such situations in 1992 as well. For example, in Sarajevo, there were enormous profits in these exchanges, because in spite of all the blockade and the siege, Sarajevo could breathe, so to speak, along the road leading to Kiseljak, although the army of Republika Srpska and the HVO was there and everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At 15.45, I had a meeting with Mr. Larry Hollingworth. He was the representative of the UNHCR. He asked me for guarantees, once again, for the safe passage of a convoy via Zepce to Maglaj. I repeated what the difficulties were in terms of communicating with the command in Zepce, and I said that I would do my best, including an open conversation on the phone with Commander Lozancic to provide guarantees and security for safe passage for the UNHCR convoy to Maglaj so that food supplies could be sent to Maglaj and to other areas where this was necessary. On the 18th of November, 1993, around 12.00, snipers from the BH army positions wounded my deputy commander Filip Filipovic but, fortunately, his wounds were not deadly. Also, I received information about the installation of a private checkpoint in Nova Bila, where criminals had set up a checkpoint and they collected money from people who wanted to pass, but I realised that the military police had reacted and dismantled this checkpoint, which meant that the road was deblocked as well. During the course of the day, I was once again in the military police unit and helping them with their training and continuing to work on the establishment of the military police. I also received a request from the hospital in Nova Bila that it was necessary to evacuate seven children as soon as possible, and 33 heavily wounded persons, and I sent this request to the command of UNPROFOR in Nova Bila. Around 10.30, I had a meeting with the commanders of brigades from the Lasva pocket, and at that meeting I announced, quite openly, to all commanders that there would be a reorganisation of the B-type special purpose units and that soldiers from that unit would be sent to the appropriate defence offices in order to get their war assignments. At this meeting, I was informed by the assistant for security that the civilian government of the municipality of Vitez had passed a decision on the purchase of weapons from military-aged men regardless of the origin of the military equipment and weapons concerned. Later, I asked for this decision to be stopped altogether because in spite of the good intentions to arm the Vitez Brigade, it led to more theft of arms and also the resale of arms which jeopardised the security situation. I sent this information, after the meeting, to the head of the main staff, that a military police had been set up, a military police of the Vitezovi special purpose unit. I asked the chief of the main staff to explain what the legal grounds was for establishing this kind of a military police, telling him that the consequence of this was the imperilment of the security situation and also the fact that my command capacity was lessened. I received an answer saying that the members of Vitezovi do not have the right to do this and that he would take care of it, together with the Minister of Defence. I also received information from the assistant for IPD that morale on the front lines was rather low and that the soldiers were exhausted, fearful, and they were panicking. At 14.20, I had a meeting with Colonel Williams. He was the commander of the British battalion of the UNPROFOR forces who replaced Colonel Duncan. At that meeting, we discussed the evacuation of the wounded or, rather, I asked him to help me in finding a way to evacuate the wounded from the church-cum-hospital, and Colonel Williams asked me whether I had any knowledge about the Geneva negotiations. I answered that I knew absolutely nothing about those negotiations. After that, Colonel Williams asked me what I knew about the military situation in Gornji Vakuf. Again, my answer was that all that I was familiar with was the situation in 20 per cent of the Travnik municipality which was under the control of the HVO and that I had no information about the military situation in Gornji Vakuf as that was the area of responsibility of the operational zone of north-western Herzegovina. We also discussed the incidents of crime in the Lasva Valley, and Colonel Williams expressed the position that there were criminal gangs in the immediate vicinity of the UNPROFOR base too which, in most cases, were stealing fuel from the tanks in the British battalion compound, and I thanked him for our cooperation until then with UNPROFOR and asked that the military police of the British battalion and that the civilian and military police of the Lasva pocket should continue their cooperation in jointly suppressing crime. At 15.00, I had a meeting with officials of the European Monitoring Mission. I know that they were based in Zenica, but I do not have any record of their names and I cannot recollect those names. They voiced their gratitude to me for the attitude of cooperation taken by the HVO towards their mission, and I asked them for information about developments in Vares. I received information that the situation in Vares was rather confusing and that a large number of refugees had left the town in the middle of winter. The European Monitoring Mission officials mentioned the possibility of the return of refugees to Vares, voicing the view that representatives of the BH army and representatives of the Bosniak Muslim authorities would not oppose this. We also discussed the question of freedom of movement, and I informed representatives of the European Monitoring Mission that in the areas within my zone of responsibility they had full freedom of movement. On the 19th of November, 1993, at 8.30, I had a briefing with my associates, and the assistant for security informed me that officers from the security service administration were visiting him again to check the results of the investigation into the crime in Ahmici. I asked at that meeting that assistance be given to the military police in supplies, logistic support, and in organising the work of the military police command, and we also discussed our regular tasks, especially regarding the security of humanitarian convoys passing through the Lasva pocket in the direction of Maglaj and Zepce under conditions when the Lasva Valley itself was suffering from hunger. I was afraid that the refugees might, on their own accord, try to attack one of those convoys. At 10.00, I had a meeting with the commanders, low-level commanders, of the military police, they were platoon and company commanders and members of the command of the military police battalion, and I requested from them that they inform me, in relation to my order, about the investigation and restoration of goods taken from the Tuzla convoy, and we also discussed reinforcements for the military police, the problems regarding the proceedings and witnesses in cases before courts because I was told that witnesses were fearful when they had to testify at the district military court against perpetrators of criminal acts. I also asked that the process of seizure of equipment and goods seized from the Tuzla convoy should continue. I also received information during the day that new units of the BH army were being brought in to the front lines at Busovaca and Vitez, and that in eight or ten days' time, a new attack of broader proportions would take place. On that day, I also visited the training centre in Nova Bila to which I had been invited by the commanders, and the problem they were encountering was food for recruits. All they had was rice and margarine and they had no bread. The same difficulties were being encountered with respect to food for the hospital in Nova Bila. They were mainly short of flour to be able to bake bread. We were also again confronted with the transfer of conscripts to the Vitezovi special purpose units and other institutions so as to avoid going to the front because the combat operations were gaining in intensity. I ordered the military police to take all necessary measures to guarantee full security for officials of the International Red Cross, the United Nations, the UNHCR, and I also requested the coordination and adjustment of procedures in assisting the district military prison if the warden of that prison were to request such assistance from the military police commander. I also received information from two surgeons -- they were the only surgeons, in fact, in the Lasva pocket -- who complained that they were being threatened when engaging in surgery by HVO soldiers who demanded that their friends had to survive operations at whatever cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps before we go on to the 20th of November -- we have been working for roughly one hour -- perhaps now would be the appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I agree. We shall have a twenty-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. The hearing will resume. Mr. Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We had stopped at the 20th of November, 1993, so please, General, continue with your presentation of the chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, on the 20th of November, 1993, I received information from my associates that we had a total of 1.698 soldiers engaged on the front line, out of which 1.175 were armed, which means that five hundred and something soldiers were without any weapons, or without barrels, as we would put it in military terms. On the 21st of November, 1993, I asked the military police and the security service to undertake additional measures to secure and protect foreign TV crews in a part of the Vitez municipality which we called The Reporters' Street. On that same day, the special purpose unit, Tvrtko, began its transformation. This was a special purpose unit of the B-type which was being reorganised, actually it was disbanded, and the soldiers from that unit were sent to the competent defence department which informed them of their new wartime assignment. I also had a meeting with the president of the district military court who again asked me to provide him with logistics support in sending soldiers to the court to be tried if such warrants should be issued by the court. For the rest of the day, I continued working on a proposal for the chief of the main staff regarding the formation of a guards unit in the Lasva Valley and the reorganisation of the existing defence system because of a major loss of territory and personnel. I addressed that document to the chief of the main staff of the HVO. Throughout that day, that is, the 21st of November, 1993, snipers and mortars were active from the BH army lines against the front line of the Vitez area. In the course of the day, I received information that the military police had seized six vehicles from a captured criminal gang, that one of those cars had been returned to its owner, whereas five had been left in the Stojkovici logistics base as it was established that they had been seized from the Tuzla convoy. I was also informed that in the direction of Stari Vitez, the Vitez Brigade had engaged about 260 soldiers in one shift for one day. These troops were blocking Stari Vitez and they had no right to engage in any kind of offensive activities against Stari Vitez. On the 22nd of November, 1993, tanks of the BH army fired at the town of Vitez and infantry attacks continued, focusing on the explosives factory. The battles went on all day and the whole communications system was damaged. I spent that day with the troops in Zaselje, and in the evening, at the forward command post in Donja Veceriska, I had a meeting with all the commanders of the defence sector of Vitez. On the 23rd of November, 1993, I received confirmation of the report that the new unit which had been formed earlier and which was called Alpha was commanded by the chief of the security service centre, Mr. Miso Mijic. I was also informed that the chief of the security service centre was detaining officers from the command of the Operative Zone and was interviewing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these were your officers, your deputies?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were my immediate associates, and I asked for an explanation from the head of the security centre, Mr. Miso Mijic, why this was being done, and he repeated again that his service was independent and that it had the authority to process, in security terms, all the military, including myself and my command. I had a meeting with an official of the UNHCR on that day, I don't remember his name, and I asked that equal treatment should be given to all in the delivery of humanitarian aid. When I say "equal treatment," I meant both for areas under control of the HVO and the areas under the control of the BH army. The commander of the Military Police Battalion informed me that stolen equipment of the Reuters TV crew had been found and that the suspect had been taken into custody, his name was Mr. Bosnjak, and that the equipment would be returned to the Reuters crew the following day. The assistant for IPD informed me, in the course of the day, that there was hunger and exhaustion among the troops, and that one of the main problems was hunger and freezing of soldiers on the front line, and that the names of conscripts that had abandoned the municipalities were being read out so as to raise the morale of the defending troops. I was informed that sniper nests had been reactivated in Stari Vitez, firing at areas under HVO control including the Vitez Hotel. The commander of the Vitez Brigade reported that criminal gangs were breaking in around town and causing chaos. These were mostly gangs coming from the area of Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Busovaca.
