On the 24th of November, 1993, I got a report from the security service that a burglary had been carried out in the food storage depot in Vitez and that a certain quantity of food had been taken away. We were still receiving information on the incidence of neuroses and exhaustion among troops on the front line. I asked the security service to report to me about the military police formed by the Vitezovi special unit, and my assistant for security told me that as far as he knew, they indeed had no right to form any military police unit. We also reviewed the question of the passage of humanitarian convoys through the Lasva Valley and the potential for security problems which we envisaged because of widespread hunger in the pocket. In the course of the day, I had a meeting with Colonel Williams and with a representative of the UNHCR, Mr. Larry Hollingworth, who informed me that a convoy with food would soon arrive from Banja Luka and Metkovic for the Central Bosnia area and that ten truckloads of food would arrive in Vitez to be distributed in the following way: Seven trucks for the part of the Vitez municipality under Croatian control, and two truckloads for Kruscica under the control of the BH army, and one truckload of food for Stari Vitez. After this meeting, I was again informed of clashes between the assistant for security and the chief of the security centre. At about 18.55, I spoke to the chief of the main staff of the HVO and informed him of these problems in the relationship between the SIS centre and the assistant for security, also about the problem regarding the role of the head of the SIS centre and the problem of command and control over special purpose units, and I asked him to speed up the resolution of all these problems. He told me, "Hold on. I will assist as much as I can. We will meet soon." About 19.30, there was another attack on Vitez and combat operations continued. On the 25th of November, 1993, a convoy consisting of about 18 trucks carrying food from the UNHCR passed through without any obstruction or difficulty. The convoy passed through towards Zenica. The commander of the Military Police Battalion informed me that the military policeman Anton Zepackic was persecuting and participating in the persecution of Muslims and their eviction from flats in Vitez. I ordered disciplinary measures to be taken against him and for this military policeman to be dismissed from the military police. This was indeed done. I asked the assistant for security to report to me regarding all my requests up to the 30th of November, 1993. The assistant for security informed me that the overall situation in the Light Assault Battalion was very poor. At 10.00, I had a meeting with all the brigade commanders in the Lasva pocket. The subject of discussion was the implementation of orders received in the month of November 1993. We discussed, in particular, the problems of the movement of soldiers from Busovaca to Vitez and vice versa, depending on where the fighting was more intensive. There were sometimes arbitrary and spontaneous drain-off of soldiers from one battlefield to another. I was also informed on that occasion about a new problem, and that is that Croats were persecuting Croatian refugees. In the villages of Krcevine and Jardol, Croat refugees from Zenica had been housed together with their families. When the need arose for some of the military conscripts to be transferred from Krcevine and Jardol to Zaselje and Gornja Veceriska, hospitality was withdrawn for those conscripts which were transferred to Zaselje and Gornja Veceriska, so that once again we had a rather complicated situation in regard to finding accommodation for displaced persons from Zenica. At a meeting which I had with the commanders, the command of the Light Assault Battalion did not attend but he sent a message that they were under the control of the military police and that they would invite me to attend a meeting at their own headquarters when they were able to organise a meeting of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, the Light Assault Battalion, what was its name previous and what type of unit was it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In fact, it was created by expanding the ATG unit, that is, the anti-terrorist group which was named the Jokers, Jokeri, and was directly subordinate to the head of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the course of the day, I received a report from the commander of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, with regard to his military police. I asked for a book regulating the formation of the special purpose unit because if it was allowed then there would be a special group for the military police, but I did not receive that book of regulations to have a look at it and the military police was still functioning. From the Military Intelligence Service I received information that preparations were under way by the BH army to launch a broader attack and that the bulk of the forces were to be engaged from Sivrino Selo and Kruscica with the aim of taking control of the explosives factory and the centre of the town of Vitez itself. I also received information, according to which the ammunition supply was being carried out in Stari Vitez via a humanitarian organisation and that payment for the BH army to that humanitarian organisation, which was to the tune of 30.000 Deutschmarks, German Marks, for one convoy carrying ammunition and payments were paid into giro accounts abroad. On the 26th of November, 1993, I once again asked the Vitezovi for their book of regulations, but I did not receive it. Sometime between 10.00 and 13.00, I was at the training centre doing training with the instructors from the centre. I talked to the commander for the security detail at the explosives factory, and the commander informed me that he had released a military policeman for looting, because they had undertaken stealing. On the 27th of November, 1993 -- that is, he had fired them -- I received a report from the military police that he had a well-trained unit to ensure the security of the convoy, and that all equipment had been returned to Reuters, and that in Busovaca an armed attack had been carried out by the members of the Light Assault Battalion on the headquarters of the company of the HVO military police in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the Light Assault Battalion, formation-wise, who did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Light Assault Battalion was within the composition of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 28th of November, the IPD workers organised at the Vitez Hotel a seminar which was, in fact, a repetition of a seminar that had been held previously for lower-ranking officers, commanders of sectors and commanders of companies. The topic discussed was international humanitarian organisations and their mission, their mandate, the mandate of the Geneva Conventions and international war law. Once again that day, I received an invitation from Mr. Abdulah Tuco, who complained to me that four HVO soldiers had asked him to leave his family home, his house, and I asked protection from the military police for that family. On the 29th of November, 1993, I received a report from the assistant for health because jaundice had broken out and there were a great many problems with relation to hygiene amongst the soldiers up at the front lines. The health assistant also complained that the seriously wounded had not been evacuated despite requests and promises that had been given and that some of the wounded people had died in the church-cum-hospital. On the 30th of November, 1993, I sent out a written report to the main headquarters of the HVO regarding the problem of theft and crime in the Lasva pocket, and I had a meeting on that same day with Mr. Tjorborn (phoen), he was a member of the European Monitoring Mission, he was an officer of that mission, and he informed me about the situation in Vares, and I informed him for my part that according to our information, the BH army had been using, in the Lasva pocket, artillery projectiles with chloride and that we had proof in the form of shrapnel, parts of these projectiles, and the findings of physicians who had examined patients. On the 1st of December, 1993, we received a threat at our headquarters, the Operative Zone command, from criminal groups, and they said that there was going to be a showdown with the military police and with the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, a settling of accounts, and we once again came up with a problem of water supplies and electricity used for wartime purposes, that is to say, we continued to be without water and without electricity in the Lasva pocket, particularly in the Novi Travnik, Vitez, and part of the Travnik municipalities, including the hospital there. On that day, an initiative was launched by the soldiers from the Vitez Brigade to form a club, a civilian association, which said that it could tackle the problem of food supplies and hunger in the Lasva pocket, and one soldier was demobilised from the Vitez municipality and Busovaca and Novi Travnik and part of the Travnik municipality, one soldier from each of these municipalities, in order to set up this sort of businessmen's association to deal with the food supply. On the 2nd of December, I was at the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade command and had a meeting there to discuss security issues up at the front line and once again to deal with crime suppression. During the 2nd of December, once again the BH army used its artillery, and as far as we knew, it used these projectiles filled with chloride, and I sent a message about this to the chief of the main staff and via the assistant for IDP and the liaison officer with UNPROFOR, I asked that a physician from the UNPROFOR British battalion go to the church-cum-hospital to examine the patients there who had been hit and injured by those projectiles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to D389, Defence Exhibit 389, dated the 1st of December, 1993. This is Defence Exhibit 389, document D389, and you sent it on the 1st of December, 1993, to a number of units in Central Bosnia and services there. The title is "Treatment of Prisoners of War - Command." (as read) "On the basis of the memorandum GS number 02-211-1-01-4117/93 of the 30th of November, 1993, in connection with the treatment of prisoners of war on the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, I hereby command: 1. In the zones of brigade responsibility, to ensure that the military prisoners of war (these are persons who bear a visible sign of belonging to enemy formation and firearms) at the time of capture are to be treated in the following manner: (a) Compulsory disarmament, taking away personal documents and sorting them by military classes, more precisely: rank and file soldiers, noncommissioned officers, officers and higher officers according to rank; (b) Military prisoners of war are sent off from the front line at least --" There's an illegible word there in the original. "-- more precisely: without fail, they must be placed outside the war zones in the district military prison of Busovaca, the OVZ of Busovaca; (c) Military prisoners of war must perform daily specified tasks and set their lodgings in order. They have the right to receive letters and prisoners' packages through the International Red Cross; (d) All evidence, legal and administrative, on the question of prisoners of war and persons who have this status must be maintained in an orderly manner and strictly kept; (e) All activities of the military prisoners of war must be justified; (f) The treatment of military prisoners of war must be within the framework of the Geneva Conventions and international law concerning the treatment of military prisoners of war. 2. Familiarise all soldiers with the contents of this command through unit commanders and PD authorities. 3. The order comes into force immediately. Commanders of brigades and independent units in ZP Vitez are responsible to me for its complete execution." Signed by Commander Tihomir Blaskic. Tell us, please, General, did you write this order, did you send it, dispatch it, because it is titled "To all units"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This order was also discussed as a subject at the seminar with the military commanders, organised by the offices of the International Red Cross and the IPD workers for the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think the order speaks for itself. We're not going to analyse it. I should just like to ask you to continue with the chronology of events now, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 3rd of December, 1993, we were confronted with an epidemic, a flu epidemic, so that I had received reports that in the space of two days, from the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski in Busovaca, 84 soldiers had gone down with the flu and were therefore not up at the front lines because they were suffering from flu, and the situation was similar in the Vitez Brigade. I was invited to a meeting that day by the commander of the light assault battalion in Busovaca, and we discussed a series of issues at the meeting. I specifically asked that they try to introduce law and order and professional military conduct in their unit and to define their internal structure and also to dovetail their conduct and the role of the unit with the existing military regulations. There were other questions under discussion like guarantees for a future in the encirclement, and I stressed in particular that regardless of the final outcome, that a state governed by law would be built up in the Central Bosnia area and in Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of anybody's personal views and stands. On the 4th of December, 1993, I wanted to finish the operative plan of the fight against crime along with coordination from my other associates, and I once again worked on the elaboration of a paper for the chief of the main staff with regard to the disbanding of the special purpose units and to abolish the A-type special purpose units in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. On the 6th of December, 1993, I had a meeting with an officer of the International Red Cross, his name was Dominik, and the questions that we discussed at the meeting were how to link up families that had been separated as a consequence of war, and I asked the representative of the International Red Cross to tell me what the standard criteria were for linking up families, bringing them back together again, but I was not given any clarification as to those criteria. What I was told was that this was done only in exceptional cases, families were reunited in exceptional cases. I also introduced the officer of the International Red Cross to the problem of the suffering of children in the Lasva pocket, and I said that we had about 100 killed and injured children in the Lasva pocket and that there were some 15.000 children up to the age of 14. I informed him about the lack of medical personnel in the Lasva pocket, the use of chemical weapons, and the hunger that we had to face in the Lasva pocket. On the 7th of December, I received permission from the chief of the main staff to engage a legal man in the commands of the brigades, and the object of these legal men was to provide professional legal assistance in disciplinary action and disciplinary measures and that in that way they should contribute to consolidating law and order and discipline generally. I also had a meeting with Colonel Williams, the commander of the British battalion attached to UNPROFOR, and with Major Lara (phoen), he was an UNPROFOR officer from the UNPROFOR command for Bosnia-Herzegovina from Kiseljak, and at the meeting we discussed the following issues: the question of water, water supply, for Novi Travnik, Nova Bila, and Vitez, and I was told that Commander Cuskic, that is to say, the commander of the 7th Krajina Brigade of the BH army, in the course of the day would switch on the water supply for Novi Travnik and Nova Bila. We also discussed the electricity problem, and I agreed to give maximum assistance for teams to be able to see to the maintenance of the electricity supply system, and I asked the colonel to convey to the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army our proposal that all combat activities be halted during the Christmas holidays and festivities and that I personally proposed that the same be done by the HVO for the Bajram festivities, that is to say, the festivities of the Muslim community members. On the 8th of December, at headquarters, we were working out the documents on planning, coordinating our work. On the 9th of December, at headquarters, we organised a methodological exercise dedicated to the work of a military disciplinary court at the level of brigade and level of Operative Zone, and we gave all the participants auxiliary documents which make it possible to initiate proceedings in terms of infractions of military discipline. Then we showed, on a practical example, how a military disciplinary court functions. During the day, I also had an open telephone conversation with commander Lozancic in Zepce, so that I would organise safe passage for 30 trucks of UNHCR aid for the town of Maglaj. On the 13th of December, 1993, I had a meeting with the UNPROFOR commander of the Nordic Battalion. It says here in my notes that his name was Harry Smith, but I'm not sure that was his name. He informed me about the situation in the town of Vares and said that in town there were about 200 Croats, that the surrounding Croat villages were torched and looted in the municipality of Vares. On the 14th of December, I received a report from the commander of the military police on the investigation concerning the looting of the Tuzla convoy. I was also informed that the vehicles from the Tuzla convoy were being recorded and that they were going back to the Stojkovici Logistics Brigade and that a special book of records has been opened for motor vehicles and for equipment that is being returned. On the 15th of December, 1993, at 15.00 I had a meeting with Mr. Budstaf (phoen) and Brian Cartner (phoen). At that meeting they asked me to inform them about a previously held meeting between General Rasim Delic and the chief of main staff of the HVO, Ante Roso, in Visoko. I told them that I had not even heard of this meeting being held and that I knew nothing in connection with that meeting. On the 17th of December, I had a meeting with Colonel Williams, commander of the UN Battalion, the British Battalion, in Vitez, at 9.30. At that meeting I was informed that the convoy Bijeli Put was being prepared and also the Convoy of Peace. The convoy called Bijeli Put was supposed to bring assistance to the Croats, and the Convoy of Peace was being organised by the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb for Bosniak Muslims in Central Bosnia. Colonel Williams also informed me that the commander of the 3rd Corps had accepted the proposal of a cease-fire that I had offered. The decision of the commander of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was that the cease-fire would start on the 23rd of December at 00.01 and it would go on until the 3rd of January at 24.00. That would be the Christmas cease-fire as accepted by the 3rd Corps commander. On the 19th of December, 1993, I worked in the command of the military police together with the members of the command and the commanders of the companies on elaborating a book for training members of the military police at the level of squad and platoon. These were internal books that we were working on. From the 19th of December until the 22nd of December, these convoys, Bijeli Put and the Convoy of Peace, arrived in Central Bosnia. On the 22nd of December, there was an ultimatum by the 3rd Corps that the Bijeli Put convoy had to be returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, General, the Bijeli Put convoy, was that the first assistance that you had received in terms of food from Croatia after you remained under siege as of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is the first assistance that we received. Within it only 32 tonnes of flour had arrived, and we were using 2 tonnes of flour per day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 22nd of December, the Bijeli Put convoy had to go back. At 5.50, early in the morning, a very intensive attack was launched by army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the direction of Zenica and from the direction of Zabrdze. The fighting went on until 23.00, and the most intensive operations took place against Krizancevo Selo and Gornja Veceriska and Zaselje. During that day, until noon, we had lost 217 soldiers, out of which 75 had been killed at Krizancevo Selo and 157 were either missing or wounded. While on the southern side toward Zabrdze and the explosives factory, a total of 60 soldiers were disabled. The aim of this attack was to take the explosives factory and the city of Vitez itself. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina managed to take Krizancevo Selo, and then the road was opened towards the town of Vitez and Stari Vitez. Simultaneously, the Bijeli Put convoy was being seen off, and they were leaving Vitez around 9.00 under fire. I was at the headquarters of the 1st Battalion over there at Impregnacija, in the direction of Krizancevo Selo. Deputy Commander Filipovic was in Donja Veceriska. During the second half of the night we exchanged places. I was in Donja Veceriska and he was in Impregnacija. At 23.00, we had to face a shortage of ammunition. I asked the chief of the main staff for assistance, and early in the morning we received 14.000 762 bullets by parachute. So this is a combat kit for 90 soldiers. This is such a small quantity. A soldier should not be sent to the front line with such a small quantity of ammunition. Throughout the 23rd of December, Radio Zenica were broadcasting calls to HVO soldiers to surrender and attacks were continued from Bukve towards Jardol, and then between Sljibcica, Krizancevo Selo and towards Stari Vitez, and from Kruscica towards Bobasi and towards the explosives factory. Once again, on the 23th of December or, rather, between the 23rd and 24th of December, during the night again I called the chief of the main staff so that he would do something from Kiseljak in order to alleviate the burden of the positions in Vitez. I said that it would be very difficult for us to hold on if these attacks continued. I also told him about the very heavy losses that were sustained and also the lack of ammunition for defending ourselves properly. On the 25th of December, we worked on the consolidation of the defence positions in Krizancevo Selo, where part of the front line went through the village itself and behind the village. We also worked on new positions in Donja Veceriska. On the 27th of December, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina carried out an attack on Polom, Radzenovici, and Busovaca. Around 01.30, attacks were continued against Zaselje from Zabrdze at the Vitez front line. On the 28th of December, 1993, Mr. Franjo Nakic, the chief of staff, toured Sector 2 of the defence of the Viteska Brigade. During this tour, he realised that half of the positions, rather, trenches had been lost in that sector. The head of that sector had not informed the commander of the Vitez Brigade about this, and we did not know either when the combat operations started and when that position was lost. So that was typical as well, that information was the not being sent about the losses sustained. On the 31st of December, I received information from the Military Intelligence Service that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had established another headquarters, another command post, in the monastery in Guca Gora for the 3rd Corps. On the 1st of January, 1994, I issued an order to the military police that they should protect immovable property in Krizancevo Selo from looting, arson, and devastation. However, it was virtually impossible to protect it from the refugees, and they could not be stopped in terms of taking away timber, blankets, food, and other supplies from that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, tell us, who took it away, and the owners of these houses and property in Krizancevo Selo, what ethnic background were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Croats were taking it away, and the owners of this property in Krizancevo Selo were also Croats. However, in spite of the efforts made, it was virtually impossible to stop this because hunger prevailed and people felt this need to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 1st of January, 12 military policemen were expelled from the military police because of lack of discipline, and because of their attitude towards their work in general, and because of thefts. On the 2nd of January, the attacks of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina continued against Vitez and in part against Busovaca also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down if possible?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The main direction was towards Prosje from Kacuni. Again, we elaborated a new plan. We tried to reorganise ourselves in the Lasva pocket, my associates and I, and we defined our defence tasks under the given conditions in terms of reorganising units and also in terms of speeding up the training of members of the military police. Then we focused on our main tasks. We said that our priority was defence, and fighting against crime, and disarming groups of criminals. Then also defining the relationship between the commander and the soldier. I'm talking about the chain of command as such. Then also resolving questions related to the theft of property, and the usurpation of apartments, and also improving reporting. We tried to persuade the subordinate commanders that it was necessary for them to give us timely and accurate information so that we would know what was actually happening, and where, so that we could command. I also asked to be given a summary report on all disciplinary action that was being taken within the brigades. Usually once a week I would spend an entire day in military police units during their training. On the 3rd of January, I dislocated my command post to Nova Bila, and during the day I received orders to report to the chief of the main staff of the HVO in Mostar. During the night of the 3rd of January, I was taken by helicopter to the main staff of the HVO. I was received by the deputy commander of the main staff of the HVO on the 5th of January. I informed the deputy chief of the main staff about the military situation, about the letters I had sent in relation to the reorganisation of HVO units in the Lasva pocket, and the need for all units to be placed under direct command, and also about problems between the centre of SIS, and the assistance for security. I also asked for clarification in terms of what I should do with vehicles and equipment from the Tuzla convoy which the military police was finding, and then they were taking this away from the people who had stolen it in the first place. I was told that for the time being that equipment and those vehicles should be concentrated in the logistics space of Stojkovici. After this meeting on the 5th of January, I was given permission to visit my family, and on the 6th of January, I went to Austria, and on the 8th of January already, the Minister of Defence asked me to come back urgently because of the situation that was getting increasingly complicated and that I had to go back to Vitez. I travelled to Austria by car, and I went back by plane and by car. On the 8th of January, I returned, as I was told to do, and I reported to the chief of the main staff of the HVO. There I was told that the establishment of a guards brigade was agreed to by the Minister of Defence and that I could reorganise special purpose units of the A-type, that is to say, the Vitezovi, and that I could also reorganise the light assault battalion to belong to the 3rd guards brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is a very important subject matter, and our working hours are about to expire now, Mr. President, so I suggest that we adjourn at this point, and perhaps we can continue tomorrow because we are getting closer to the end of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you where you were. I am talking about the end of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. We are getting closer to the end. So on the whole, we would not need more than three or four hours, and then I think that we could conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, we can expect to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If we have another witness tomorrow, then we couldn't tomorrow.

utterances.text: Tomorrow another witness will come, and it may last for the whole day. We are going to hear this witness in a closed session. I hope we won't spend the whole day on this witness. Anyway, we will resume tomorrow at 10.00.
